text: "I tell you the truth: whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber.
The one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
When he has brought out all his own, he goes on ahead of them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.
They will never follow a stranger; they will run from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers."
Jesus told them this figure of speech, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
So Jesus said to them again, "Truly, truly, I tell you: I am the gate for the sheep.

versions.text: So Jesus said again, "I tell you the truth: I am the gate for the sheep.
versions.explanation: The Greek includes αὐτοῖς ("to them"), which identifies the audience after the narrator's aside in verse 6. Including it also reads more naturally aloud, restoring the addressee before the renewed discourse.

versions.text: So Jesus said to them again, "I tell you the truth: I am the gate for the sheep.
versions.explanation: The Greek has the emphatic doubled ἀμὴν ἀμήν, a solemn formula characteristic of this Gospel. "I tell you the truth" conveys the sense but flattens the doubling; "Truly, truly, I tell you" preserves the emphasis and the rhythmic repetition, which is effective when read aloud.

text: All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.
I am the gate. Whoever enters through me will be saved; he will come in and go out and find pasture.
The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life, and have it in abundance.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
The hired hand, who is not the shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep and runs away—and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.
He runs away because he is only a hired hand, and the sheep mean nothing to him.

versions.text: He runs because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep.
versions.explanation: The added verb "He runs" is a reasonable bridge from verse 12, but "cares nothing for the sheep" flattens οὐ μέλει αὐτῷ περὶ τῶν προβάτων ("the sheep are no concern of his"). Sharpening the contrast makes the reason for his flight clearer and reads with better rhythm.

text: I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me,
just as the Father knows me and I know the Father—and I lay down my life for the sheep.
I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd.
This is why the Father loves me: because I lay down my life in order to take it up again.
No one takes it from me; I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I received from my Father."
Again the Jews were divided because of these words.
Many of them said, "He is possessed by a demon and out of his mind. Why listen to him?"
Others said, "These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
Then came the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem. It was winter, [Footnote: The Feast of Dedication celebrated the rededication of the temple; it is also known as Hanukkah.]

versions.text: Then came the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem. It was winter,
versions.explanation: "Feast of Dedication" is accurate but unfamiliar to many hearers. A short explanatory footnote gives helpful background without altering the text read aloud.

text: and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon's Colonnade.
The Jews gathered around him and said, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly."
Jesus answered them, "I have told you, and you do not believe. The works I do in my Father's name testify about me,
but you do not believe, because you are not among my sheep.
My sheep listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me.
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish; no one will snatch them out of my hand.
My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of the Father's hand. [Footnote: Some manuscripts read: "What my Father has given me is greater than all."]

versions.text: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of the Father's hand.
versions.explanation: The Greek text here has a well-known textual variation: one reading makes the Father the subject ("greater than all"), another makes the gift the subject ("what my Father has given me is greater than all"). A brief footnote alerts the reader without changing the main rendering.

text: I and the Father are one."
Again the Jews picked up stones to stone him.
Jesus said to them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of them are you going to stone me?"
The Jews answered, "We are not stoning you for any good work, but for blasphemy—because you, a mere man, make yourself God."
Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law: 'I said, you are gods'?
If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—
then how can you say to the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?
If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me.
But if I am doing them, then even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
Again they tried to seize him, but he slipped out of their hands.
Then he went back across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing in the early days, and he stayed there.
Many came to him, and they said, "John never performed a sign, but everything John said about this man was true."
And many believed in him there.
